title: What EPA Section 608 certification do HVAC and refrigeration technicians need?
description: EPA Section 608 technician certification under 40 CFR 82.161: Type I, II, III and Universal, exam rules, 70 percent pass mark, apprentices and card records.
shortAnswer: Under 40 CFR 82.161, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requires anyone who could reasonably be expected to breach the refrigerant circuit while maintaining, servicing, repairing or disposing of stationary refrigeration and air conditioning equipment to pass an EPA-approved certification exam. There are four types: Type I for small appliances, Type II for high-pressure, Type III for low-pressure, and Universal for all three. Certification does not expire, and certificates must be kept at the place of business.
keyTakeaways: Since January 1, 2018, certification covers work on appliances containing any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant, such as HFCs.

Type I covers small appliances, Type II medium, high and very high-pressure appliances, Type III low-pressure appliances, and Universal all of these. Motor vehicle air conditioning is certified separately under Section 609.
Each test has at least 25 core questions and 25 questions per technical type. The pass mark is 70 percent for closed-book tests and 84 percent for mail-in Type I tests.
Apprentices are exempt only while closely and continually supervised by a certified technician.
Technicians must keep a copy of their certificate at their place of business until three years after they stop working as a technician.
regulator: US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), under section 608 of the Clean Air Act
appliesTo: Technicians who maintain, service, repair or dispose of stationary refrigeration and air conditioning appliances containing class I, class II or non-exempt substitute refrigerants
Employers of HVAC, refrigeration and appliance service technicians
Apprentices working under a certified technician's supervision
Organizations that train and certify technicians under EPA-approved programs

blocks.text: Any person who could reasonably be expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit during maintenance, service, repair or disposal of a covered appliance must pass a certification exam offered by an approved program. The requirement is in [40 CFR 82.161(a)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/82.161), part of the refrigerant management rules in 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F.

EPA's [certification requirements page](https://www.epa.gov/section608/section-608-technician-certification-requirements) explains the activities that make someone a technician: attaching and detaching hoses and gauges to measure pressure, adding refrigerant to or removing it from an appliance, and any other activity that violates the integrity of a motor vehicle air conditioner (MVAC)-like appliance or small appliance, other than disposal.

Coverage widened on January 1, 2018. Before that date the section applied only to appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants (ozone-depleting substances). From that date it applies to appliances containing any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant, which brings most HFC equipment into scope.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 40 CFR 82.161 as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as at November 2026; the section text dates from 81 FR 82363 (November 18, 2016). A 2020 rule rescinded the extension of leak repair duties to substitute refrigerants but, as EPA states, did not rescind technician certification for substitutes. The 2024 HFC management rules in 40 CFR Part 84, Subpart C contain no separate technician certification section.

sections.heading: What are the four Section 608 certification types?

blocks.text: Section 82.161(a)(1) sets four types, each matched to equipment pressure class. A technician needs the type that matches every appliance they work on, or Universal to cover all of them.

items: **Type I:** persons who maintain, service or repair small appliances.
**Type II:** persons who maintain, service, repair or dispose of medium, high or very high-pressure appliances, except small appliances, MVACs and MVAC-like appliances.
**Type III:** persons who maintain, service, repair or dispose of low-pressure appliances.
**Universal:** persons who work on all appliances in the three types above.

blocks.text: Two boundary rules matter. Technicians working on MVAC-like appliances may hold either Type II or Section 609 certification under 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart B, while persons servicing MVACs for consideration must hold Section 609 certification. Persons who only dispose of small appliances, MVACs and MVAC-like appliances do not need certification.

sections.heading: How is the Section 608 exam built and scored?

blocks.text: Tests are assembled from an EPA question bank released only to approved programs. Under section 82.161(c), each test must include at least 25 questions from the core group and at least 25 from each relevant technical group, so a Universal test has 100 questions, which may be taken at once or by combining passing scores on separate Type I, II and III tests.

[Appendix D to Subpart F](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/40/appendix-D_to_subpart_F_of_part_82) sets administration standards. Type II, Type III and Universal tests are closed-book and proctored in a secure environment, with at least one registered proctor for every 50 people testing at the same time, and proctors must check photo identification. Type I may also be offered in a mail-in format, but mail-in Type I results cannot count toward Universal certification.

The passing score is 70 percent for closed-book Type I, Type II, Type III and Universal tests, and 84 percent for mail-in Type I tests. Programs must issue a wallet-sized card within 30 days of the test, showing the program name and EPA approval date, the technician's name, the certification type and a unique number that is not the technician's social security number.

Section 82.161(b)(3) encourages tests in other languages or with a translator, and requires an oral test for anyone who requests it in writing at least 30 days before the exam with an explanation. That provision is useful for crews where written English is a barrier; the general principles are in [how to make eLearning accessible](/guides/how-to-make-elearning-accessible).

sections.heading: What are the rules for apprentices and employers?

blocks.text: Apprentices are exempt from certification only while they are closely and continually supervised by a certified technician during any work that could reasonably be expected to release refrigerant. Under section 82.161(a)(2), the supervising technician and the apprentice share responsibility for the apprentice's compliance.

The rule places the certification duty on the individual, but employers carry the practical risk because uncertified staff breaching a refrigerant circuit puts the business out of compliance. EPA may require technicians to demonstrate proper recovery and recycling procedures at their place of business, and failure to demonstrate or to use equipment properly may lead to revocation or suspension of the certificate. A revoked technician must recertify before doing covered work again.

For employers, a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) that records each technician's certification type against the equipment classes they are dispatched to is the simplest control against assigning a Type I holder to a high-pressure system.

sections.heading: How do Section 608 duties map to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: For an HVAC or refrigeration contractor, the duties split between the technician, the apprentice, and the certifying organization. This original grid sets out who holds each one and what an EPA inspector visiting the business would reasonably expect; section 82.161 remains the authority.

sections.heading: Does Section 608 certification expire, and what records are kept?

blocks.text: Section 608 certification does not expire. EPA's certification requirements page states that Section 608 Technician Certification credentials do not expire, and section 82.161(a)(5) reserves the Administrator's right to require recertification in future by Federal Register notice.

Technicians must keep a copy of their certificate at their place of business and maintain it until three years after they stop operating as a technician. Since January 1, 2018, certifying organizations other than federally run programs must publish online a list of all technicians they certified on or after January 1, 2017, with name, city of residence when tested, certification types and dates, updated at least annually and with an opt-out.

Because the credential never lapses, knowledge can drift as refrigerants and rules change. Employers who want current competence rather than a historic pass may add their own refresher, using the approach in [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the Section 608 core and technical test topics to concepts and assessment points, then links each technician's certification type to the equipment classes in their role. Because federal certification does not expire, the framework also supports employer-set refreshers that target changes such as new substitute refrigerants.

faqs.q: Can a Type I open-book certificate be upgraded to Universal?
faqs.a: Not directly. Appendix D states that mail-in format Type I tests cannot be used toward Universal certification, and EPA's page states that core tests taken open book cannot be used to get Universal certification. The core test must be taken as a proctored exam.

faqs.q: Do I need Section 608 certification to service car air conditioning?
faqs.a: No. Persons who service motor vehicle air conditioners for consideration must be certified under Section 609 rules in 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart B. MVAC-like appliances can be serviced with either Type II or Section 609 certification.

faqs.q: What if I lose my Section 608 card?
faqs.a: EPA does not issue certification cards; approved certifying programs do. EPA publishes steps for replacing a lost card and lists certifying organizations that replace cards. Because programs must keep records and publish lists of technicians certified since 2017, the issuing program is the place to start.

faqs.q: Does Section 608 certification cover HFC refrigerants?
faqs.a: Yes. From January 1, 2018, section 82.161 applies to appliances containing any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant. EPA confirms that its 2020 rule rescinding leak repair duties for substitutes did not rescind the technician certification requirement.
